html:
Western Sahara is a thinly peopled desert territory on the Atlantic coast of north-west Africa, between Morocco and Mauritania. Its status has been disputed since Spain left in 1976, and it is often called Africa's last colony. The map shows it from 1945, when it was still Spanish Sahara.

As Spain withdrew, Morocco and Mauritania divided the land between them, though the International Court of Justice had found that neither had sovereignty over it. The Polisario Front, fighting for Sahrawi independence, proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic and fought both. Mauritania gave up its claim in 1979. Morocco took most of the territory, including the towns and the phosphate mines, and in the 1980s built a long sand wall, the Berm, to keep Polisario out.

Tens of thousands of Sahrawis live in refugee camps around Tindouf in Algeria, which backs Polisario. A UN ceasefire in 1991 promised a referendum on independence that has never been held. Fighting resumed in 2020. The UN mission there, MINURSO, ended in November 2026 when the Security Council failed to renew it.
